title: The Dewdrop's Song
markdown:
Willow Creek School buzzed with a quiet morning energy, like a sleepy bumblebee stretching its wings. Sunlight, still shy and misty, dappled through willow leaves onto the well-swept path and made dancing patterns. Inside the small cozy radio station, which smelled of old paper and warm dust, Ms Flint adjusted her glasses. Her programme, Morning Melodies and More, was famous for calm music and cheerful announcements. Her notes were neat. Her microphone gleamed.

“Good morning,” Ms Flint began, voice like warm honey on buttered toast. “This is Ms Flint with Morning Melodies and More on Willow Creek Radio. A beautiful day is dawning. Like a canvas painted with the softest light. Ideal for learning, for a bit of quiet thinking, and for enjoying the gentle rhythm of the day. And now, for the weather report.” She tapped her microphone, a tiny crisp gesture of waiting. “We’re expecting sunshine with a gentle breeze. Just the sort of weather that makes squirrels chase each other up trees and children skip along the paths. The temperature will be a pleasant…”

A sound. A tiny, almost musical plink-plink-plonk. Delicate, like a raindrop trying to learn a tune on a lily pad. Soft, yet it cut through the quiet.

Ms Flint paused. Her neat hair did not dare move. “Hmm. That’s a funny noise.” She leaned closer. Plink-plink-plonk. “A rather strange little sound. Perhaps a very small bird practising scales in the eaves? Or a mischievous cricket with a tiny violin?” She gave a small chuckle.

Down by the whispering creek, Bea the beaver was smoothing the last twig on her dam. Her whiskers twitched with satisfaction. Strong, neat, perfectly watertight. Then she heard it, a faint echo on the breeze. Plink-plink-plonk. Not the gurgle of water, nor the rustle of leaves, nor a robin.

“Now this is strange,” Bea murmured, practical paws on a perfectly placed pebble. “My dam is sound. No leaks, no wobbles. That little tune is not part of the usual creek symphony.” She wiggled her nose, trying to catch the scent of the sound.

A little further along, where reeds swayed like dancers, Sol the swan practised his graceful glides, neck curved like a question mark. His sharp ears caught the same delicate sound. Tiny bells made of dew.

“That’s very odd,” Sol mused, tilting his head. “It has a certain charm. Wistful. Tinkling. Not a frog’s croak, nor a duck’s quack, nor the sigh of wind through the reeds.”

Back at the station, Ms Flint grew subtly puzzled. She adjusted a dial, then another. “Well, the little musical interlude seems to have stopped. A mystery. We shall keep our ears open. And now, a spot of music…”

Before she could reach for her selection, the plink-plink-plonk returned, a little louder, a tiny tug on her sleeve. She peered at the soundboard. Knobs and lights offered no explanation.

“It seems our weather report is being accompanied by a rather persistent tiny orchestra,” she said, amusement replacing puzzlement. “Perhaps the sunshine has its own special song today.”

Bea, organised and practical, decided this peculiar happening called for an investigation. She carefully packed away her tools and followed the sound. Her paws padded softly on the damp earth, leading her away from the comforting neatness of her perfect dam toward the grand old oak that stood like a watchful guardian near the school building. Sol, elegant neck craning, curiosity thoroughly piqued, followed the delicate melody too. His graceful stride carried him closer to the sounds of the schoolyard, his own quiet search underway.

The plink-plink-plonk grew clearer. It came from a small mossy alcove at the base of the oak, often overlooked, carpeted with emerald moss and dotted with tiny wildflowers. Bea and Sol arrived at almost the same moment. Their eyes met with a shared silent question.

And there, nestled among dew-kissed moss, sat a single perfect dewdrop. It shimmered with miniature rainbow colours, catching the soft morning light. As it wobbled in the breeze, it made that distinctive plink-plink-plonk. Not a bird. Not an insect. A lost dewdrop, fallen from its cloud, trying with all its tiny might to sing its way home.

They did not rush. For a moment they only watched. The oak held its breath. The moss held the drop. The drop held the morning.

“Oh, you poor little thing,” Bea whispered, practical nature melting. Her whiskers drooped with sympathy.

“You must be trying to signal your family,” Sol added, voice a soft murmur. “A song of longing for the puffy clouds.”

The dewdrop pulsed with a faint internal glow, as if it understood. It wobbled again, a soft hopeful plink.

Bea, with careful precision, nudged a fallen leaf toward it: broad, perfectly shaped, a tiny shimmering slide. Sol, with a soft controlled puff from his beak, made a gentle gust. Together they guided the dewdrop onto the leaf. Then, with a final hopeful plink-plonk like a tiny farewell bell, it began its journey, glistening upward on the faint morning breeze, a sparkling adventurer rising toward cloudy home.

At the radio station, Ms Flint heard the plink-plink-plonk fade, replaced by the soft sigh of wind through willows. A peaceful quiet settled over the airwaves.

“Ah,” she said, a genuine smile reaching her eyes. “It seems our little musical mystery has resolved itself. The dewdrop has sung its farewell.” She paused. “And wouldn’t you know it, the sun is indeed shining, and the breeze is just as we predicted. A perfect day.”

Bea returned to her dam with a new wonder that had nothing to do with perfect construction. Sol returned to his elegant glides, heart a little lighter. Ms Flint returned to her ordered programme, her voice carrying a touch of the dewdrop’s gentle melody. On the oak’s moss the alcove was empty, still dotted with wildflowers, and the morning, for a moment, still listened. The creek chuckled on. The willow leaves made their dancing patterns. Somewhere above the school, a cloud had one small singer home.
characters: Bea (a dam-building beaver), Sol (an elegant creek swan), Ms. Flint (a honey-voiced radio host)
